text:
**Short answer:** Yes, at about $450 or less, if you want a well-tested ~1 kWh unit for outages and camping and will mostly run AC loads. At $499 or more, newer models are a better buy.

**Buy it:** [BLUETTI AC180 at BLUETTI US](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603) lists it at $499 with a 5-year warranty and a 30-day price match. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BLUETTI+AC180) showed $449 in the iTechGuides roundup, and WattPowerStation noted $449 on the brand store. Prices vary by listing, so check the current one.

**What's good**
- **Real capacity:** Six independent tests measured 82–90% of the rated 1,152 Wh, roughly 950–1,030 Wh. That is good for the class ([WattPowerStation](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/), [PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- **Power:** It puts out 1,800 W continuous and 2,700 W in Power Lifting mode, which suits heating loads only.
- **Battery:** LiFePO4 rated for 3,500+ cycles, with a 5-year warranty.
- **Charging:** About 1.3–1.8 hours from the wall in Turbo mode, and up to 500 W of solar input ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- **Extras:** It has a wireless charging pad and UPS-style backup.

**What's not**
- **Weight:** At about 36 lb, it is heavy for its capacity. OutdoorGearLab scored it only 66/100 and criticized its power-to-weight ratio and noisy fan.
- **Small loads:** Efficiency drops sharply at low draw. Outdoor Life measured only 54% of rated capacity at about 34 W, so it's a weaker pick for a CPAP or an overnight fridge. DC efficiency was also mediocre at 71% ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- **Expansion:** Bluetti's page advertises B80, B230 and B300 expansion batteries. Other sources say it has no true expansion port and can only be topped up from them in Power Bank Mode ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac180), [WattPowerStation](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). Confirm this with Bluetti before buying if expansion matters to you.
- **Heat:** Output drops to 1,500 W above 95°F ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **UPS setting:** An app setting called Grid Enhancement can prevent backup from working, so turn it off if you use the UPS function.

**Alternatives:** OutdoorGearLab calls the successor, the Bluetti Elite 100 V2, a better product. It's lighter (25 lb), quieter, and charges faster, with 1,024 Wh of capacity. It costs around $489 per WattPowerStation. OutdoorGearLab also favors the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (about $499.99). I didn't get buy links for either, so check current prices on [WattPowerStation's comparison](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/).

**Verdict:** Buy the AC180 if you find it at about $400–$450. Otherwise, the Elite 100 V2 or Anker C1000 Gen 2 is likely the better deal at similar money.

Dealectric lists a 5% code, AFF5OFF, that it says worked in Bluetti's cart. It's an affiliate site, so use the code only if it applies at checkout.
